`````text
1	# Authoring patterns
2	
3	Condensed from <https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices>. Read this
4	before writing or editing a SKILL.md body.
5	
6	## Table of contents
7	
8	1. [Spending context wisely](#spending-context-wisely)
9	2. [Cross-agent frontmatter compatibility](#cross-agent-frontmatter-compatibility)
10	3. [Calibrating control](#calibrating-control)
11	4. [Gotchas sections](#gotchas-sections)
12	5. [Output templates](#output-templates)
13	6. [Checklists for multi-step workflows](#checklists-for-multi-step-workflows)
14	7. [Validation loops](#validation-loops)
15	8. [Plan-validate-execute](#plan-validate-execute)
16	9. [Bundling reusable scripts](#bundling-reusable-scripts)
17	10. [Quick checklist before commit](#quick-checklist-before-commit)
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Spending context wisely
22	
23	Every token in `SKILL.md` competes with the conversation history, the system
24	prompt, and every other active skill. Spend tokens on what the agent **wouldn't
25	know without you**:
26	
27	- Project-specific conventions (table names, repo layout, internal jargon)
28	- Domain-specific procedures with non-obvious steps
29	- Edge cases the agent will misjudge by default
30	- Specific tools/APIs to prefer (with the *why*, briefly)
31	
32	Don't spend tokens on:
33	
34	- Explaining what well-known things are (PDF, HTTP, REST, JSON)
35	- Generic "best practices" the agent already applies (handle errors, write tests)
36	- Comprehensive option enumerations — give a default and one escape hatch
37	
38	**Test:** for each paragraph, ask "would the agent get this wrong without it?"
39	If no, cut it.
40	
41	### Progressive disclosure
42	
43	Three loading levels:
44	
45	| Level | Loaded | Budget |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| Frontmatter (`name`, `description`) | always | 120-500 chars preferred, 1024 max |
48	| `SKILL.md` body | when skill triggers | <500 lines, <5000 tokens |
49	| `references/*.md`, `assets/*`, `scripts/*` | on demand | unlimited |
50	
51	If `SKILL.md` is creeping past 500 lines, move sections to `references/<topic>.md`
52	and reference them with **load conditions** ("Read X if Y happens"), not just
53	"see X for details". Conditions let the agent load on demand; bare pointers tend
54	to either get ignored or get pre-loaded out of caution.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## Cross-agent frontmatter compatibility
59	
60	Use this as the portable baseline for coding agents that consume Agent Skills:
61	
62	- `name`: required, lowercase letters/digits/hyphens only, no leading/trailing
63	  hyphen, no `--`, <=64 characters.
64	- `description`: required, non-empty string, <=1024 characters. Include both
65	  what the skill does and concrete trigger contexts. Keep the first 60
66	  characters meaningful because `npx skills` truncates picker hints there.
67	- **Quoting**: a YAML plain (unquoted) scalar may not contain `": "`, and ` #`
68	  starts a comment. Long English descriptions hit both constantly
69	  (`"…debug a FastAPI app: choosing def vs async def"`). Wrap such values in
70	  single quotes — the whole skill is otherwise skipped at install time with
71	  "Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings", or installs with a
72	  silently truncated description. `scripts/lint-frontmatter.sh` gates this.
73	- Keep `name` and `description` as the only required frontmatter fields for
74	  portability. Agent-specific fields are allowed when needed, but isolate them
75	  intentionally: Cursor uses `disable-model-invocation`, Codex can read
76	  `agents/openai.yaml`, and some vendored skills carry upstream-only metadata.
77	
78	Description budget tiers:
79	
80	| Tier | Length | Meaning |
81	|---|---:|---|
82	| Green | 120-500 chars | Preferred for local skills: enough trigger surface without context bloat |
83	| Yellow | 501-900 chars | Valid, but context-heavy; move details to `SKILL.md` body |
84	| Orange | 901-1024 chars | Valid, but close to hard loader limits |
85	| Red | >1024 chars | Invalid for Codex/Cursor/spec-aligned validators |
86	
87	Agent notes:
88	
89	- **Codex** skips invalid `SKILL.md` files; OpenAI's validator enforces the
90	  64-char name and 1024-char description limits.
91	- **Cursor** managed `create-skill` guidance matches the same 64/1024 limits
92	  and supports `disable-model-invocation` for explicit-only skills.
93	- **Claude Code** uses descriptions for discovery and tolerates additional
94	  frontmatter in practice, but long descriptions still consume always-on
95	  context and are poor picker hints.
96	- **OpenCode** follows the Agent Skills convention and uses descriptions for
97	  invocation; stay within the portable baseline unless a target agent's docs
98	  say otherwise.
99	- **Claude.ai upload** may impose stricter UI limits. Treat that as a separate
100	  packaging target, not the default coding-agent baseline for this repo.
101	
102	---
103	
104	## Calibrating control
105	
106	Match instruction specificity to **task fragility**, not to "we should be thorough".
107	
108	### Be prescriptive when:
109	
110	- The operation is destructive or has side effects
111	- A specific sequence of steps must hold (migration, release, deploy)
112	- An external system requires exact format (API contract, parser input)
113	
114	```markdown
115	## Database migration
116	
117	Run exactly this sequence:
118	
119	    python scripts/migrate.py --verify --backup
120	
121	Do not modify the command or add flags. The `--verify` step seeds an
122	integrity check that later phases depend on.
123	```
124	
125	The trailing sentence is the trick — even when prescriptive, **explain why**.
126	Agents that understand the reason follow it more reliably than agents that just
127	see "DO NOT" in caps.
128	
129	### Give the agent freedom when:
130	
131	- Multiple valid approaches exist
132	- The output is judgment-driven (code review, refactor proposal)
133	- You'd be hand-coding policy if you wrote it all out
134	
135	```markdown
136	## Code review process
137	
138	1. Check database queries for SQL injection (use parameterized queries)
139	2. Verify auth checks on every endpoint
140	3. Look for race conditions in concurrent code paths
141	4. Confirm error messages don't leak internals
142	```
143	
144	Notice: *what to look for*, not *how to look for it*. The agent picks the
145	approach.
146	
147	### Defaults, not menus
148	
149	When several tools could work, pick one default and mention alternatives as
150	escape hatches.
151	
152	```markdown
153	Use pdfplumber for text extraction.
154	
155	For scanned PDFs requiring OCR, fall back to pdf2image with pytesseract.
156	```
157	
158	…not:
159	
160	```markdown
161	You can use pypdf, pdfplumber, PyMuPDF, or pdf2image depending on...
162	```
163	
164	### Procedures over declarations
165	
166	Teach the agent *how* to approach the class of problem, not *what* to produce
167	for one instance.
168	
169	```markdown
170	Bad — only useful for this exact query:
171	  Join `orders` to `customers` on `customer_id`, filter region='EMEA',
172	  sum `amount`.
173	
174	Good — works for any query:
175	  1. Read schema from `references/schema.yaml` to find relevant tables.
176	  2. Join via the `_id` foreign key convention.
177	  3. Apply user-requested filters as WHERE clauses.
178	  4. Aggregate numeric columns and format as a markdown table.
179	```
180	
181	Specifics still belong in the skill (output format templates, "never output
182	PII", tool-specific quirks) — but the *approach* should generalize.
183	
184	---
185	
186	## Gotchas sections
187	
188	Often the single highest-value section in a skill. **Concrete corrections to
189	mistakes the agent will make without being told.** Not generic advice.
190	
191	```markdown
192	## Gotchas
193	
194	- The `users` table uses soft deletes. Queries must include
195	  `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` or results will include deactivated accounts.
196	- The user ID is `user_id` in the database, `uid` in the auth service, and
197	  `accountId` in the billing API. All three refer to the same value.
198	- The `/health` endpoint returns 200 if the web server is up, even if the
199	  database is down. Use `/ready` to check full service health.
200	```
201	
202	Keep gotchas in `SKILL.md`, not in a separate reference. The whole point is
203	that the agent reads them **before** hitting the situation — by the time it
204	realizes it should load `references/gotchas.md`, the bug has happened.
205	
206	**Iteration tip:** every time you correct the agent during a real run, add the
207	correction here. Most skills' gotchas sections grow over weeks, not get written
208	all at once.
209	
210	---
211	
212	## Output templates
213	
214	Agents pattern-match against concrete structures more reliably than they
215	follow prose descriptions. When the output has a fixed shape, paste the shape:
216	
217	````markdown
218	## Report structure
219	
220	Use this template, adapting sections as needed:
221	
222	```markdown
223	# [Analysis Title]
224	
225	## Executive summary
226	[One paragraph]
227	
228	## Key findings
229	- Finding 1 with supporting data
230	- Finding 2 with supporting data
231	
232	## Recommendations
233	1. Specific actionable recommendation
234	2. Specific actionable recommendation
235	```
236	````
237	
238	Long templates or templates that only apply in some cases should live in
239	`assets/<name>.template` and be loaded on demand from `SKILL.md`.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Checklists for multi-step workflows
244	
245	Make dependencies and validation gates visible:
246	
247	```markdown
248	## Form processing workflow
249	
250	Progress:
251	- [ ] 1. Analyze the form  → `scripts/analyze_form.py`
252	- [ ] 2. Create field mapping  → edit `fields.json`
253	- [ ] 3. Validate mapping  → `scripts/validate_fields.py`
254	- [ ] 4. Fill the form  → `scripts/fill_form.py`
255	- [ ] 5. Verify output  → `scripts/verify_output.py`
256	```
257	
258	The agent treats the checkboxes as state and won't skip to step 4 without
259	ticking 1-3. Dependency arrows make the wiring explicit.
260	
261	---
262	
263	## Validation loops
264	
265	For tasks where output quality is testable, instruct the agent to validate
266	and re-try, not "do your best and stop":
267	
268	```markdown
269	## Editing workflow
270	
271	1. Make your edits.
272	2. Run validation: `python scripts/validate.py output/`
273	3. If validation fails:
274	   - Read the error message.
275	   - Fix the issues.
276	   - Run validation again.
277	4. Only proceed when validation passes.
278	```
279	
280	The validator can be a script, a reference checklist, or a self-check prompt.
281	The pattern is identical: **do → validate → fix → re-validate → proceed**.
282	
283	---
284	
285	## Plan-validate-execute
286	
287	For batch or destructive operations, force the agent through an intermediate
288	**plan artifact** that gets validated before any side effects happen:
289	
290	```markdown
291	## PDF form filling
292	
293	1. Extract form fields:
294	   `python scripts/analyze_form.py input.pdf`  → `form_fields.json`
295	2. Create `field_values.json` mapping each field name to its intended value.
296	3. Validate:
297	   `python scripts/validate_fields.py form_fields.json field_values.json`
298	   (checks every field exists, types match, required fields present)
299	4. If validation fails, revise `field_values.json` and re-validate.
300	5. Fill the form:
301	   `python scripts/fill_form.py input.pdf field_values.json output.pdf`
302	```
303	
304	The magic is step 3. A validator that catches "field 'signature_date' not
305	found — available: customer_name, order_total, signature_date_signed" lets the
306	agent self-correct **before** the destructive step 5.
307	
308	This pattern eliminates an entire class of "oops, ran the wrong thing on prod"
309	failures. Use it any time the actual operation is hard to undo.
310	
311	---
312	
313	## Bundling reusable scripts
314	
315	When you iterate on a skill (with `skill-creator`), watch the agent transcripts
316	across test runs. If the agent independently reinvents the same logic each run
317	— building the same chart, parsing the same format, validating the same way —
318	that's a signal to write the script once and bundle it in `scripts/`.
319	
320	Heuristic: if you see the same ~20-line helper appearing in 2+ runs, bundle it.
321	
322	See `references/script-design.md` for **how** to design bundled scripts so an
323	agent can call them reliably.
324	
325	---
326	
327	## Quick checklist before commit
328	
329	Before considering a SKILL.md "done":
330	
331	- [ ] Description includes specific trigger contexts ("use when X, Y, Z"),
332	      not just a one-line summary
333	- [ ] Description is "pushy" but within budget: 120-500 chars preferred,
334	      <=1024 chars required
335	- [ ] First 60 description chars are useful in picker UIs
336	- [ ] Name is hyphen-case and <=64 chars
337	- [ ] SKILL.md is under 500 lines (move overflow into `references/`)
338	- [ ] Every `references/*.md` is mentioned with a load condition, not just
339	      listed at the bottom
340	- [ ] Has a `## Gotchas` section (or an honest reason it's empty)
341	- [ ] Output format, if structured, is shown as a literal template
342	- [ ] Multi-step procedures use checklists with dependencies marked
343	- [ ] Destructive operations go through plan-validate-execute or have
344	      `--dry-run` support
345	- [ ] Bundled scripts are listed under `## Available scripts` with their flags
346	- [ ] No "MUST" / "ALWAYS" / "NEVER" in caps without an accompanying *why*
347
`````
</details></tool-use>

````text
1	# pueued daemon setup and configuration
2	
3	The `pueue` client is a thin RPC frontend; all state lives in `pueued`. If
4	the daemon isn't running, every `pueue` invocation fails with a connection
5	error. This page covers: getting `pueued` running per-OS, the config knobs
6	worth setting, where logs live, and how to run an isolated daemon for tests.
7	
8	## Starting `pueued`
9	
10	### Once-off
11	
12	```bash
13	pueued -d
14	```
15	
16	`-d` daemonizes (detaches from the terminal). Without `-d`, `pueued` runs in
17	the foreground — useful only for debugging.
18	
19	### Auto-start on login
20	
21	#### macOS (launchd)
22	
23	Create `~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.nukesor.pueued.plist`:
24	
25	```xml
26	<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
27	<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
28	<plist version="1.0">
29	<dict>
30	    <key>Label</key>
31	    <string>io.github.nukesor.pueued</string>
32	    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
33	    <array>
34	        <string>/opt/homebrew/bin/pueued</string>
35	    </array>
36	    <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
37	    <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
38	    <key>StandardOutPath</key>
39	    <string>/tmp/pueued.out.log</string>
40	    <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
41	    <string>/tmp/pueued.err.log</string>
42	</dict>
43	</plist>
44	```
45	
46	Then:
47	
48	```bash
49	launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.nukesor.pueued.plist
50	launchctl start io.github.nukesor.pueued
51	```
52	
53	Adjust the `pueued` path if you installed via `cargo install` or a non-Homebrew prefix (`which pueued`).
54	
55	#### Linux (systemd-user)
56	
57	Create `~/.config/systemd/user/pueued.service`:
58	
59	```ini
60	[Unit]
61	Description=pueue daemon
62	After=default.target
63	
64	[Service]
65	Type=simple
66	ExecStart=%h/.cargo/bin/pueued
67	Restart=on-failure
68	
69	[Install]
70	WantedBy=default.target
71	```
72	
73	Adjust `ExecStart` to your actual `pueued` path. Then:
74	
75	```bash
76	systemctl --user daemon-reload
77	systemctl --user enable --now pueued
78	journalctl --user -u pueued -f      # tail logs
79	```
80	
81	#### Windows
82	
83	Pueue ships a Windows service installer in newer releases. See
84	`https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue/wiki` for current instructions —
85	auto-start on Windows historically required a wrapper.
86	
87	## Config file location
88	
89	| OS | Path |
90	|---|---|
91	| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/pueue.yml` |
92	| Linux | `~/.config/pueue/pueue.yml` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pueue/pueue.yml`) |
93	| Windows | `%APPDATA%\pueue\pueue.yml` |
94	
95	The file is auto-created on first daemon start with sensible defaults.
96	Override with `pueued -c /path/to/pueue.yml` or `PUEUE_CONFIG_PATH`.
97	
98	## Important config knobs
99	
100	```yaml
101	# pueue.yml
102	shared:
103	  pueue_directory: ~/Library/Application Support/pueue   # where state + logs live
104	  use_unix_socket: true                                  # macOS/Linux only
105	
106	daemon:
107	  default_parallel_tasks: 1                              # initial slots for `default` group
108	  pause_group_on_failure: true                           # ← set this!
109	  pause_all_on_failure: false                            # nuclear: pauses every group on any failure
110	  callback: null                                         # optional shell command run on task done
111	  callback_log_lines: 10
112	  groups:
113	    default: 1                                           # parallelism per group
114	    ml: 4
115	    io: 2
116	
117	client:
118	  read_local_logs: true
119	  show_confirmation_questions: false
120	  edit_cmd: ["vim", "-f"]                                # what `pueue edit` opens
121	  show_expanded_aliases: false
122	  status_time_format: "%H:%M:%S"
123	  status_datetime_format: "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
124	```
125	
126	### `pause_group_on_failure: true`
127	
128	**Strongly recommended.** When any task in a group fails, the daemon pauses
129	the whole group — no new tasks start until you `pueue start --group G`.
130	This prevents a cascade of failures (e.g. all 30 sweep tasks failing
131	because of a missing env var) before you've noticed.
132	
133	There is **no CLI flag** for this — it's config-only. After editing the
134	file, restart the daemon: `pueue shutdown && pueued -d`. Or `pueue reset`
135	to wipe state and reload.
136	
137	### `default_parallel_tasks`
138	
139	Slots for the `default` group on first daemon launch. Once the group
140	exists, this value is ignored — set per-group with `pueue parallel N
141	--group default` (or via the `groups:` block above).
142	
143	### `groups:` block
144	
145	Pre-declare groups + their parallelism. Equivalent to running `pueue group
146	add` + `pueue parallel` for each one. Useful for declarative
147	machine-provisioning (chezmoi, Ansible, etc.).
148	
149	### `callback`
150	
151	Shell command run after every task finishes. Receives `$PUEUE_TASK_ID`,
152	`$PUEUE_GROUP`, `$PUEUE_RESULT`, `$PUEUE_INPUT` (the command), and a few
153	other env vars. Use case: send a notification, post to Slack, append to
154	an audit log.
155	
156	## Where logs live
157	
158	| OS | Path |
159	|---|---|
160	| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/logs/` |
161	| Linux | `~/.local/share/pueue/logs/` (or `$XDG_DATA_HOME/pueue/logs/`) |
162	| Windows | `%APPDATA%\pueue\logs\` |
163	
164	Each task gets one file: `<task_id>.log`. Reading directly is faster than
165	`pueue log --json --full <id>` for huge logs (the JSON form loads
166	everything into memory).
167	
168	## Isolated daemon for tests
169	
170	To run pueued without disturbing your normal queue:
171	
172	```bash
173	TMPDIR=$(mktemp -d)
174	mkdir -p "$TMPDIR/state" "$TMPDIR/config"
175	cat > "$TMPDIR/config/pueue.yml" <<EOF
176	shared:
177	  pueue_directory: $TMPDIR/state
178	  use_unix_socket: true
179	daemon:
180	  default_parallel_tasks: 4
181	  pause_group_on_failure: true
182	EOF
183	PUEUE_CONFIG_PATH="$TMPDIR/config/pueue.yml" pueued -d
184	sleep 1
185	PUEUE_CONFIG_PATH="$TMPDIR/config/pueue.yml" pueue add -- echo isolated
186	```
187	
188	The `tests/conftest.py` fixture in this skill uses this pattern.
189	
190	## Stopping the daemon
191	
192	```bash
193	pueue shutdown    # graceful
194	```
195	
196	State persists. The next `pueued -d` resumes where you left off (queued
197	tasks remain queued, running tasks were killed during shutdown so they
198	typically need a `pueue restart --in-place`).
199	
200	## Troubleshooting
201	
202	- **"Connection refused" or "couldn't connect"** — `pueued` not running.
203	  `pueued -d`, or `scripts/check-daemon.sh --start`.
204	- **"Version mismatch"** — client and daemon versions differ. Restart the
205	  daemon (`pueue shutdown && pueued -d`).
206	- **Tasks stuck in `Queued` forever** — group might be paused. Check
207	  `pueue group --json` for `"status": "Paused"`. Resume with `pueue start
208	  --group G`.
209	- **`pueued -d` exits silently** — usually means the socket is held by an
210	  old/zombie daemon. Check `pgrep -lf pueued`; kill stragglers; remove the
211	  socket file under `pueue_directory/`.
212	- **Logs missing** — `pueue log <id>` falls back to in-memory if the file
213	  is gone. To preserve logs across `pueue clean`, copy them out of the log
214	  dir before cleaning.
215
````
</details></tool-use>

````text
1	# pueue JSON schema (observed on 4.0.2)
2	
3	Pueue's JSON output is **not formally documented** in the wiki. This page
4	captures the shape observed on **pueue 4.0.2** (macOS, but the shape is
5	identical across platforms — only paths differ). If `pueue --version`
6	reports a different major version, re-verify with the diagnostic command at
7	the bottom.
8	
9	## `pueue status --json`
10	
11	Top-level shape:
12	
13	```json
14	{
15	  "tasks": {
16	    "<id>": { ...task object... },
17	    ...
18	  },
19	  "groups": {
20	    "<group_name>": {
21	      "status": "Running" | "Paused" | "Reset",
22	      "parallel_tasks": <int>      // 0 = unlimited
23	    },
24	    ...
25	  }
26	}
27	```
28	
29	### Task object fields
30	
31	| Field | Type | Notes |
32	|---|---|---|
33	| `id` | int | Stable while the task exists. Reused only after `pueue clean`/`reset`. |
34	| `created_at` | string (ISO-8601) | When `pueue add` was called. |
35	| `original_command` | string | Exactly what was passed to `pueue add`. |
36	| `command` | string | Post-shell-substitution form (often equal to `original_command`). |
37	| `path` | string | Working directory at submit time. |
38	| `envs` | object | Captured env vars at submit time. |
39	| `group` | string | Group name. `"default"` if not specified. |
40	| `dependencies` | int[] | Empty `[]` if no `--after`. Order matches the `--after` flags. |
41	| `priority` | int | 0 if not set. Higher = sooner. |
42	| `label` | string \| null | The `--label` value. `null` if not given. |
43	| `status` | object | Tagged enum, see below. |
44	
45	### `status` (tagged enum)
46	
47	The outer key is the variant name; the inner object has the variant's data.
48	
49	#### `Stashed`
50	
51	```json
52	{"Stashed": {"enqueue_at": null}}
53	{"Stashed": {"enqueue_at": "2026-04-27T...+08:00"}}   // delayed
54	```
55	
56	#### `Queued`
57	
58	```json
59	{"Queued": {"enqueued_at": "2026-04-27T...+08:00"}}
60	```
61	
62	#### `Running`
63	
64	```json
65	{"Running": {"enqueued_at": "...", "start": "..."}}
66	```
67	
68	#### `Paused`
69	
70	Pauses a Running task; carries the same fields as Running plus a pause time.
71	
72	#### `Locked`
73	
74	Rare — used during edit/restart transitions.
75	
76	#### `Done`
77	
78	```json
79	{
80	  "Done": {
81	    "enqueued_at": "2026-04-27T11:01:06.893055+08:00",
82	    "start": "2026-04-27T11:01:07.003813+08:00",
83	    "end": "2026-04-27T11:01:07.307972+08:00",
84	    "result": <result>
85	  }
86	}
87	```
88	
89	`result` takes one of:
90	
91	| Value | Meaning |
92	|---|---|
93	| `"Success"` | exit 0 |
94	| `"DependencyFailed"` | a parent in `dependencies` failed; this task never ran (`start == end`) |
95	| `"Killed"` | someone called `pueue kill` |
96	| `{"Failed": <int>}` | non-zero exit; the int is the exit code |
97	| `{"FailedToSpawn": "<os error>"}` | OS-level launch failure — the task never ran. **Dict-shaped, not a bare string** (verified on 4.0.2). Most common cause when driving a remote daemon: the recorded working directory doesn't exist on the daemon's host. |
98	
99	`result` is a tagged enum, so treat **anything terminal that is not `"Success"`
100	as a failure**. Matching against a list of known-bad variants lets an
101	unrecognized one (as `FailedToSpawn` once did) silently count as success —
102	`wait.py` uses the allowlist form for this reason.
103	
104	### `groups`
105	
106	```json
107	{
108	  "default":   {"status": "Running", "parallel_tasks": 1},
109	  "ml":        {"status": "Running", "parallel_tasks": 4},
110	  "frozen":    {"status": "Paused",  "parallel_tasks": 2}
111	}
112	```
113	
114	`parallel_tasks=0` means unlimited.
115	
116	## `pueue log --json`
117	
118	Shape:
119	
120	```json
121	{
122	  "<id>": {
123	    "task": { ...same task object as in status... },
124	    "output": "<full stdout/stderr stream as a single string>"
125	  },
126	  ...
127	}
128	```
129	
130	`pueue log --json` (no `--full`) returns only the last few lines of `output`.
131	`--full` returns everything (loaded into RAM — beware for huge logs; in that
132	case, read the file directly from `~/Library/Application Support/pueue/logs/`
133	on macOS or `~/.local/share/pueue/logs/` on Linux).
134	
135	## Pueue's built-in QUERY DSL (prefer over jq for simple filters)
136	
137	`pueue status [QUERY]` accepts a SQL-ish filter string that the daemon
138	applies *before* serialization — faster than jq on a big task table, and
139	shorter to type. Works with `--json`. Documented under `pueue status --help`.
140	
141	Grammar:
142	
143	```
144	[columns=[col,...]]?  [filter ...]*  [order_by col asc|desc]?  [first|last N]?
145	
146	cols accepted in columns=[]:    id, status, command, label, path,
147	                                enqueue_at, dependencies, start, end
148	cols accepted in filters:       status, command, label, start, end, enqueue_at
149	filter ops:                     =   !=   <   >   %=   (%= = "contains")
150	```
151	
152	Recipes:
153	
154	```bash
155	# Last 10 failed tasks across all groups, with end time
156	pueue status --json 'status=Failed order_by end desc first 10'
157	
158	# Substring match on label (great for label-prefix workflows)
159	pueue status --json 'label %= sweep-'
160	
161	# Currently running tasks (no enum value for Running here — use jq for state),
162	# but for any Done variant (Success, Failed, Killed, DependencyFailed) the DSL works:
163	pueue status --json 'status=Success last 20'
164	
165	# Compose: failed in the last hour, project columns
166	pueue status --json 'status=Failed end > 2026-04-27T00:00:00Z columns=[id,label,end]'
167	
168	# Order by start, take the most recent 5
169	pueue status --json 'order_by start desc first 5'
170	```
171	
172	The DSL covers ~80% of common queries with one-line incantations. For
173	status-enum *variant* matching that the DSL doesn't expose (e.g.
174	`Running`, `Stashed`, `DependencyFailed` specifically) or complex
175	projections, fall back to `jq` (next section).
176	
177	## Useful `jq` recipes
178	
179	```bash
180	# All currently-running task ids
181	pueue status --json | jq '[.tasks | to_entries[] | select(.value.status | has("Running")) | .key | tonumber]'
182	
183	# All failed tasks (label + exit code)
184	pueue status --json | jq '
185	  .tasks | to_entries[] | select(.value.status.Done.result | type == "object" and has("Failed"))
186	  | {id: .key, label: .value.label, exit_code: .value.status.Done.result.Failed}
187	'
188	
189	# All DependencyFailed tasks
190	pueue status --json | jq '
191	  .tasks | to_entries[]
192	  | select(.value.status.Done.result == "DependencyFailed")
193	  | {id: .key, label: .value.label, deps: .value.dependencies}
194	'
195	
196	# Pending count per group
197	pueue status --json | jq '
198	  .tasks | to_entries
199	  | map(select(.value.status | has("Queued")))
200	  | group_by(.value.group) | map({group: .[0].value.group, pending: length})
201	'
202	
203	# Direct dependents of task 17
204	pueue status --json | jq '[.tasks | to_entries[] | select(.value.dependencies | index(17)) | .key | tonumber]'
205	
206	# Tasks finished in the last hour, sorted by end time desc
207	pueue status --json | jq --arg cutoff "$(date -u -v-1H +%FT%TZ 2>/dev/null || date -u -d '-1 hour' +%FT%TZ)" '
208	  [.tasks | to_entries[]
209	   | select(.value.status.Done? and (.value.status.Done.end >= $cutoff))]
210	  | sort_by(.value.status.Done.end) | reverse
211	  | map({id: .key, label: .value.label, result: .value.status.Done.result})
212	'
213	```
214	
215	## Verify on your version
216	
217	If you're on a different major version, run this once and diff against the
218	shapes above:
219	
220	```bash
221	# Submit a quick probe task, check raw shape
222	pueue add --print-task-id --label probe-schema -- 'true'
223	sleep 1
224	pueue status --json | jq '.tasks | to_entries[] | select(.value.label == "probe-schema") | .value | keys'
225	pueue status --json | jq '.tasks | to_entries[] | select(.value.label == "probe-schema") | .value.status'
226	# cleanup
227	ID=$(pueue status --json | jq -r '.tasks | to_entries[] | select(.value.label == "probe-schema") | .key' | tail -n1)
228	pueue remove "$ID"
229	```
230	
231	If the keys or status shape differ, update `wait.py` and `submit.sh`
232	accordingly — both already handle the documented variants but a new variant
233	(e.g. a hypothetical `Suspended`) will fall into the "Unknown" bucket of the
234	summary.
235
````
</details></tool-use>

1	"""Tests for scripts/submit.sh — single-task pueue submission."""
2	from __future__ import annotations
3	
4	import json
5	import subprocess
6	
7	from conftest import pueue_status, wait_for_terminal
8	
9	
10	def run_submit(env, *args):
11	    """Run submit.sh against the isolated daemon and return parsed JSON."""
12	    cmd = ["bash", str(env["__SUBMIT_SH"]), *args]
13	    r = subprocess.run(cmd, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
14	    return json.loads(r.stdout), r
15	
16	
17	def test_submit_minimal(pueue_env, scripts_dir):
18	    pueue_env["__SUBMIT_SH"] = str(scripts_dir / "submit.sh")
19	    result, proc = run_submit(pueue_env, "--label", "t-min", "--", "true")
20	    assert isinstance(result["task_id"], int)
21	    assert result["label"] == "t-min"
22	    assert result["group"] == "default"
23	    assert result["after"] == []
24	    assert result["immediate"] is False
25	
26	    st = wait_for_terminal(pueue_env, [result["task_id"]])
27	    task = st["tasks"][str(result["task_id"])]
28	    assert task["status"]["Done"]["result"] == "Success"
29	
30	
31	def test_submit_with_after(pueue_env, scripts_dir):
32	    pueue_env["__SUBMIT_SH"] = str(scripts_dir / "submit.sh")
33	    parent, _ = run_submit(pueue_env, "--label", "parent", "--", "true")
34	    child, _ = run_submit(
35	        pueue_env, "--label", "child", "--after", str(parent["task_id"]), "--", "true",
36	    )
37	    assert child["after"] == [parent["task_id"]]
38	    st = wait_for_terminal(pueue_env, [parent["task_id"], child["task_id"]])
39	    assert st["tasks"][str(child["task_id"])]["dependencies"] == [parent["task_id"]]
40	    assert st["tasks"][str(child["task_id"])]["status"]["Done"]["result"] == "Success"
41

44	    pueue_env["__SUBMIT_SH"] = str(scripts_dir / "submit.sh")
45	    parent, _ = run_submit(pueue_env, "--label", "fail-parent", "--", "false")
46	    child, _ = run_submit(
47	        pueue_env, "--label", "fail-child", "--after", str(parent["task_id"]), "--", "true",
48	    )

51	    child_result = st["tasks"][str(child["task_id"])]["status"]["Done"]["result"]
52	    assert isinstance(parent_result, dict) and "Failed" in parent_result
53	    assert child_result == "DependencyFailed"

````text
1	# Completion contracts
2	
3	Designing a record of "this finished, and here is how it went" that outlives
4	the agent, the session, and the queue.
5	
6	## Why this exists
7	
8	The agent's context is the least durable place in the system. It is lost to
9	session exit, compaction, a dropped SSH connection, a closed laptop, or an OOM
10	in the harness itself. If the only evidence that Phase A succeeded lives there,
11	the recovery path is re-running the GPU time.
12	
13	The filesystem and the scheduler's accounting database both outlive the agent.
14	Put the record there.
15	
16	## The atomic marker
17	
18	```bash
19	python train.py > runs/v2.log 2>&1
20	rc=$?
21	printf '%s\n' "$rc" > runs/v2.exit.tmp && mv runs/v2.exit.tmp runs/v2.exit
22	```
23	
24	**Write to a temp name, then `mv`.** Within a single filesystem `mv` is a
25	`rename(2)`, which is atomic: a concurrent reader sees either no marker or a
26	complete one, never a half-written one. A plain `> runs/v2.exit` can be
27	observed empty between `open` and `write`, and an empty marker read as an exit
28	code is a silent success.
29	
30	Two ways this breaks:
31	
32	- **Across filesystems** `mv` degrades to copy-then-unlink and loses atomicity.
33	  Keep the `.tmp` in the same directory as the final marker — not in `/tmp`.
34	- **The writer dies before the `mv`.** By design: no marker means *unknown*,
35	  which is the correct reading.
36	
37	`scripts/run-and-mark.sh` implements this, plus a `.meta` sidecar with the
38	command, host, timestamps, and pid.
39	
40	## Absence is not success
41	
42	The single most important rule when reading markers back:
43	
44	| Observed | Means | Do |
45	|---|---|---|
46	| marker present, `0` | succeeded | proceed |
47	| marker present, non-zero | failed | report the code and the log |
48	| **no marker, never started** | not started | start it |
49	| **no marker, but started** | **unknown** — killed, node died, still running | **ask; do not re-run silently** |
50	
51	`check-runs.sh` distinguishes the last two and exits `4` on unknown. Treating
52	unknown as "not done, so re-run" is how people accidentally launch a second
53	copy of an eight-hour job that is still running.
54	
55	## Slurm: exit codes that outlive the queue
56	
57	`scontrol show job <id>` is **live only** — the record disappears once the job
58	ages out of the controller's memory. For anything you will read later, use
59	`sacct`, which reads the accounting store.
60	
61	```bash
62	sacct -j "$JID" --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS --parsable2
63	```
64	
65	### State vocabulary
66	
67	| State | Meaning |
68	|---|---|
69	| `COMPLETED` | *"Job has terminated all processes on all nodes with an exit code of zero."* |
70	| `FAILED` | *"Job terminated with non-zero exit code or other failure condition."* |
71	| `CANCELLED` | *"Job was explicitly cancelled by the user or system administrator. The job may or may not have been initiated."* |
72	| `TIMEOUT` | *"Job terminated upon reaching its time limit."* |
73	| `OUT_OF_MEMORY` | *"Job experienced out of memory error."* |
74	| `NODE_FAIL` | *"Job terminated due to failure of one or more allocated nodes."* |
75	| `PREEMPTED` | *"Job terminated due to preemption."* |
76	| `BOOT_FAIL` | *"Job terminated due to launch failure, typically due to a hardware failure"* |
77	| `DEADLINE` | *"Job terminated on deadline."* |
78	| `REQUEUED` | *"Job was requeued."* |
79	
80	`TIMEOUT`, `OUT_OF_MEMORY`, `NODE_FAIL`, and `PREEMPTED` are the four that mean
81	**"retry might work"** — as opposed to `FAILED`, which usually means your code
82	is wrong. Distinguishing them is the difference between a useful automated
83	retry and an infinite loop.
84	
85	### ExitCode field
86	
87	- `ExitCode` — *"The exit code returned by the job script or salloc, typically
88	  as set by the exit() function."*
89	- `DerivedExitCode` — *"The highest exit code returned by the job's job steps
90	  (srun invocations)."*
91	- Format is `exitcode:signal` — *"Following the colon is the signal that caused
92	  the process to terminate if it was terminated by a signal."*
93	
94	This is why `sbatch --wait`'s exit code is not enough on its own: it collapses
95	*every* signal death to `1`. A `137` (SIGKILL, usually OOM) and a deliberate
96	`exit 1` are the same number to the caller. `sacct`'s `State` plus the `:signal`
97	suffix recovers the distinction.
98	
99	### If accounting is not configured
100	
101	`sacct` needs an accounting store — *"the job accounting log file or Slurm
102	database, as configured with the AccountingStorageType parameter"*. On a
103	cluster without `slurmdbd`, `sacct` may return nothing.
104	
105	That is precisely the case where your **own** marker file is the system of
106	record, not a nicety. If `sacct -j "$JID"` comes back empty on a job you know
107	ran, stop relying on it and write markers.
108	
109	## Shared filesystems
110	
111	On NFS/Lustre/GPFS — i.e. every cluster — a marker written by a compute node is
112	not instantly visible on the login node. NFS caches file attributes
113	(`acregmin`/`acregmax`, typically a few seconds up to a minute) and provides
114	only close-to-open consistency.
115	
116	Practical consequences:
117	
118	- A watcher can observe "no marker" for some seconds *after* the job wrote one.
119	  Keep timeouts generous; never treat a single missing-marker observation as
120	  proof of failure.
121	- Have the writer `close()` the file before the reader looks — the
122	  temp-file-then-`mv` pattern gives you this, since `mv` happens after close.
123	- Do not build tight loops around marker appearance; you are polling a cache.
124	
125	If you need a *fast* completion signal on a cluster, the scheduler is the
126	better source (`sacct`, or a Tier 0 dependency that never needs a signal at
127	all). Markers are for durability, not latency.
128	
129	## Waiting primitives and their portability
130	
131	Which of these you can actually use depends on the OS, and the answers are not
132	symmetric.
133	
134	| Primitive | Works on | Notes |
135	|---|---|---|
136	| `wait "$PID"` | everywhere | **Children of the current shell only.** Cannot wait on a foreign pid. |
137	| `tail --pid=PID -f /dev/null` | GNU coreutils only | BSD/macOS `tail` rejects `--pid` outright. On macOS with Homebrew coreutils it is `gtail`. |
138	| `pidwait` | Linux, procps-ng | Not on macOS. |
139	| `inotifywait` | Linux, inotify-tools | **Races**: if the marker already exists when it starts, it blocks forever. Test first, then watch. |
140	| `fswatch` | macOS/Linux, but not preinstalled | |
141	| `flock` | Linux (util-linux) | Not on stock macOS. |
142	| `until <check>; do sleep N; done` | everywhere | Polling — and that is fine, because it is outside the model's context. |
143	
144	**The design rule that falls out of this table:** own the process, or own a
145	marker. Attaching to a stranger's PID has no portable answer, so do not build
146	on it. `run-and-mark.sh` runs the command as its own child specifically so that
147	plain `wait` — the one primitive available everywhere — is sufficient.
148	
149	If you must watch a marker rather than a process, the race-free shape is:
150	
151	```bash
152	until [ -f "$MARKER" ]; do sleep 10; done     # test-then-sleep, not watch-then-hope
153	```
154	
155	Boring, portable, correct, and free — as long as the model is not the thing
156	doing the looping.
157
````
</details></tool-use>

1	---
2	name: herdr
3	description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
4	---
5	
6	# Herdr
7	
8	Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.
9	
10	Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:
11	
12	```bash
13	test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
14	```
15	
16	If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.
17	
18	When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.
19	
20	## Learn the current CLI
21	
22	The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:
23	
24	```bash
25	herdr --help
26	```
27	
28	Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:
29	
30	```bash
31	herdr agent
32	herdr pane
33	herdr workspace
34	herdr tab
35	herdr worktree
36	herdr terminal
37	herdr notification
38	herdr integration
39	herdr session
40	herdr machine
41	```
42	
43	Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.
44	
45	Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.
46	
47	## Understand layout, panes, and agents
48	
49	Choose the primitive that matches the job:
50	
51	- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
52	- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
53	- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.
54	
55	A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.
56	
57	Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced. Suspending an agent with Ctrl+Z and running a non-agent command preserves its identity while the exact process remains alive. This does not preserve the original identity across another recognized agent taking over. A retained identity does not mean the agent is in the foreground; inspect the pane before sending input.
58	
59	`idle` and `done` normally indicate the agent is ready for input; neither guarantees that an unfamiliar approval dialog was recognized or that a retained agent is in the foreground. The CLI/API uses the server's seen state to distinguish them; explicit focus commands mark the target seen, while reads do not. Each TUI client tracks viewed completions independently, so its Done badge can differ from the CLI or another client's badge. Antigravity and Grok can be idle while background tasks or subagents keep running, so a settled-state wait is not proof those jobs have finished. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.
60	
61	## Use IDs and caller context
62	
63	Public IDs are opaque stable handles:
64	
65	- workspace: `w1`
66	- tab: `w1:t1`
67	- pane: `w1:p1`
68	
69	Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.
70	
71	Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:
72	
73	```bash
74	printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
75	```
76	
77	Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. An omitted `pane split` target uses the calling pane when `HERDR_PANE_ID` is available, otherwise the focused pane. Other commands may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.
78	
79	Discover live state with:
80	
81	```bash
82	herdr workspace list
83	herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
84	herdr pane current --current
85	herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
86	herdr agent list
87	```
88	
89	Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.
90	
91	IDs and live agent names are scoped to one server. Two saved SSH machines can both have `w1:p1` or an agent named `reviewer`. Selecting a machine in the TUI does not retarget commands running in your pane: without `--machine`, they still use the inherited session and socket context.
92	
93	To control a saved SSH machine, use the same global prefix for discovery and every later command:
94	
95	```bash
96	herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent list
97	herdr --machine <label-or-id> pane list
98	herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent prompt <remote-agent-name> "Reply with your current status." --wait --timeout 120000
99	```
100	
101	The selector must be an enabled saved profile ID or a unique, case-sensitive label, not an arbitrary SSH hostname. Commands use that profile's remote session without an open TUI. Do not combine `--machine` with `--session` or `--remote`. Discover IDs on that machine; inherited local IDs and `--current` do not identify remote panes.
102	
103	Both installations must support machine API forwarding, and the remote server must already be running and API-compatible. Forwarding never installs, starts, or restarts a server and never falls back to Local. Local configuration, session management, installation commands, and interactive attachment are not forwarded. Remote worktree paths must be absolute, `~`, or start with `~/`; plugin link paths must be absolute. A connection failure does not prove a mutation was not applied: inspect remote state before retrying.
104	
105	`herdr machine list` lists saved connection profiles, not a cross-machine pane inventory; add `--json` for scripts. Only add, remove, enable, or disable profiles when the user asks. Removing a profile disconnects the client but does not stop remote sessions. Interactive `machine add` discovers running remote sessions and may ask the user to pick one; non-interactive setup uses the remote default session unless `--remote-session` is explicitly supplied. Use `herdr machine status [<label-or-id>] --json` to diagnose a failing machine. `herdr machine reconnect` needs the user to complete SSH authentication in their terminal; do not run it for them. Setup asks before stopping an incompatible server and defaults to No; do not approve replacement without the user's consent. Experimental handoff is not part of `machine add`.
106	
107	## Start and coordinate an agent
108	
109	Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.
110	
111	Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:
112	
113	```bash
114	herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
115	```
116	
117	Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:
118	
119	```bash
120	herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
121	```
122	
123	Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.
124	
125	An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:
126	
127	```bash
128	herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
129	```
130	
131	Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:
132	
133	```bash
134	herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
135	```
136	
137	A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.
138	
139	Submit work through the agent surface:
140	
141	```bash
142	herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
143	```
144	
145	`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter as one ordered submission. It reports successful submission only after both have been written; that alone does not prove the agent started a turn. For Codex on Windows, Herdr sends a paste boundary before Enter so submission does not depend on prompt size. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.
146	
147	With `--wait`, a prompt sent from a non-working state must produce observed `working` or `blocked` activity. After submission, Herdr waits up to five seconds for that activity; unrelated `idle`, `done`, or session changes do not satisfy this gate. It returns `agent_prompt_stalled` if no activity is observed, or `timeout` if the caller's timeout expires first. The caller timeout includes submission time. Without a timeout, the settled-state wait is indefinite after activity is observed. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.
148	
149	Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:
150	
151	```bash
152	herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
153	```
154	
155	Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.
156	
157	Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:
158	
159	```bash
160	herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
161	herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
162	```
163	
164	Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:
165	
166	```bash
167	herdr agent get reviewer
168	herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
169	```
170	
171	If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. A timeout or stalled response does not prove the prompt was never delivered; do not blindly submit it again. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.
172	
173	## Run an ordinary command in another pane
174	
175	Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:
176	
177	```bash
178	herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
179	```
180	
181	Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:
182	
183	```bash
184	herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
185	herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
186	herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
187	```
188	
189	`pane run` queues command text and Enter together; success acknowledges admission, not command execution. On macOS, `pane run` and `agent start` reject a command that exceeds the terminal's current canonical line-input limit before queuing it. Wait for the interactive shell prompt before retrying. The check covers this submission, not an earlier incomplete line or a later terminal-mode change. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.
190	
191	Use the read source that matches the task:
192	
193	- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
194	- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
195	- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
196	- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.
197	
198	Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.
199	
200	`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. Alternate-screen rows do not enter ordinary host scrollback. For supported idle agents, Herdr can collect application-owned history and restore the viewport afterward, but not every application or response can be recovered this way.
201	
202	If a larger recent read still does not reveal the completed response, ask the agent to write it as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read that file on the same machine. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.
203	
204	## Safety and coordination rules
205	
206	- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
207	- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
208	- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
209	- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked. Ordinary CLI/API closes do not inherit the TUI's last-pane confirmation. `workspace close --group` closes the primary workspace and its linked worktree workspaces; never add it merely to bypass `workspace_group_close_required`.
210	- Use `--trust-repository` only after the user has verified the repository. It grants per-request Git trust; it is not a routine retry for a failed worktree command.
211	- Client and server versions can differ after an update. Check `herdr status` before relying on new server features. A missing method is not permission to stop or upgrade a server.
212	- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
213	- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
214	- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.
215

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# check-daemon.sh — verify pueued is reachable and emit a JSON health summary.
3	#
4	# Bash 3.2 compatible (works on stock macOS).
5	
6	set -euo pipefail
7	
8	usage() {
9	  cat <<'EOF'
10	Usage: check-daemon.sh [OPTIONS]
11	
12	Probe whether `pueued` is running and the `pueue` client can reach it.
13	Emit a JSON summary to stdout; prose hints to stderr.
14	
15	Options:
16	  --start            Auto-launch `pueued -d` if the daemon is unreachable.
17	                     Re-checks afterward. No-op if already running.
18	  --json             Emit JSON to stdout (default; flag kept for symmetry).
19	  --help, -h         Show this help and exit.
20	
21	Examples:
22	  check-daemon.sh
23	  check-daemon.sh --start | jq -r .daemon_running
24	
25	Exit codes:
26	  0  daemon healthy
27	  2  `pueue` CLI not on PATH
28	  3  daemon unreachable (and --start was not given, or start failed)
29	  4  client/daemon version mismatch (rare; restart pueued to fix)
30	EOF
31	}
32	
33	log()  { printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2; }
34	warn() { printf 'warn: %s\n' "$*" >&2; }
35	die()  { printf 'error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit "${2:-1}"; }
36	
37	START=0
38	
39	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
40	  case "$1" in
41	    --start) START=1; shift ;;
42	    --json)  shift ;;
43	    --help|-h) usage; exit 0 ;;
44	    *) die "unknown flag: $1 (try --help)" 1 ;;
45	  esac
46	done
47	
48	# --- 1. Is the pueue CLI installed?
49	if ! command -v pueue >/dev/null 2>&1; then
50	  log "pueue CLI not found on PATH. Install:"
51	  log "  macOS:   brew install pueue"
52	  log "  Linux:   cargo install --locked pueue   (or distro package)"
53	  log "  Windows: see https://github.com/Nukesor/pueue#installation"
54	  printf '{"daemon_running":false,"error":"pueue_not_installed"}\n'
55	  exit 2
56	fi
57	
58	CLIENT_VERSION=$(pueue --version 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}')
59	
60	# --- 2. Detect platform + log dir.
61	PLATFORM=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
62	case "$PLATFORM" in
63	  darwin)  LOG_DIR="${HOME}/Library/Application Support/pueue/logs" ;;
64	  linux)   LOG_DIR="${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/pueue/logs" ;;
65	  *)       LOG_DIR="(unknown for $PLATFORM — check pueued config)" ;;
66	esac
67	
68	# --- 3. Probe the daemon. `pueue status --json` returns non-zero if unreachable.
69	probe_daemon() {
70	  pueue status --json 2>/dev/null
71	}
72	
73	STATUS_JSON=$(probe_daemon || true)
74	
75	if [ -z "$STATUS_JSON" ]; then
76	  if [ "$START" = "1" ]; then
77	    log "daemon unreachable — attempting: pueued -d"
78	    if ! command -v pueued >/dev/null 2>&1; then
79	      log "pueued binary not on PATH (pueue CLI was, but daemon binary is separate)"
80	      printf '{"daemon_running":false,"error":"pueued_not_installed"}\n'
81	      exit 3
82	    fi
83	    # Detach so we don't block. nohup avoids inheriting stop-on-terminal-close.
84	    nohup pueued -d </dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 &
85	    # Give it a moment to bind the socket.
86	    sleep 1
87	    STATUS_JSON=$(probe_daemon || true)
88	    if [ -z "$STATUS_JSON" ]; then
89	      log "started pueued but it's still unreachable. Check ~/Library/Application Support/pueue/ (macOS) or ~/.local/share/pueue/ (Linux) for stale socket or config errors."
90	      printf '{"daemon_running":false,"error":"start_failed"}\n'
91	      exit 3
92	    fi
93	    log "pueued started."
94	  else
95	    log "pueued not running. Start with: pueued -d   (or rerun with --start)"
96	    printf '{"daemon_running":false,"error":"daemon_unreachable","platform":"%s","client_version":"%s"}\n' \
97	      "$PLATFORM" "$CLIENT_VERSION"
98	    exit 3
99	  fi
100	fi
101	
102	# --- 4. Emit health summary as JSON.
103	# We use python3 to compose the JSON safely from the status payload.
104	PUEUE_STATUS_JSON="$STATUS_JSON" \
105	PUEUE_CLIENT_VERSION="$CLIENT_VERSION" \
106	PUEUE_PLATFORM="$PLATFORM" \
107	PUEUE_LOG_DIR="$LOG_DIR" \
108	python3 <<'PY'
109	import json, os
110	status = json.loads(os.environ["PUEUE_STATUS_JSON"])
111	groups = status.get("groups", {})
112	default_group = groups.get("default", {})
113	out = {
114	    "daemon_running": True,
115	    "client_version": os.environ["PUEUE_CLIENT_VERSION"],
116	    "platform": os.environ["PUEUE_PLATFORM"],
117	    "log_dir": os.environ["PUEUE_LOG_DIR"],
118	    "default_group": {
119	        "parallel_tasks": default_group.get("parallel_tasks"),
120	        "status": default_group.get("status"),
121	    },
122	    "groups": {name: {"parallel_tasks": g.get("parallel_tasks"), "status": g.get("status")}
123	               for name, g in groups.items()},
124	    "task_count": len(status.get("tasks", {})),
125	}
126	print(json.dumps(out))
127	PY
128

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# cleanup.sh — prune pueue task history, empty groups, and old log files.
3	#
4	# Pueue's task list grows unbounded — `pueue status --json` walks the whole
5	# table and gets slower over time. Empty groups left behind from
6	# `--isolated-group` runs accumulate too. This script wraps the safe
7	# subset of cleanup operations and emits a JSON report of what it touched.
8	#
9	# Bash 3.2 compatible (works on stock macOS).
10	
11	set -euo pipefail
12	
13	usage() {
14	  cat <<'EOF'
15	Usage: cleanup.sh [OPTIONS]
16	
17	Prune pueue state. Safe by default — only `pueue clean` (which leaves
18	running/queued tasks untouched) runs unless other flags are given.
19	
20	Options:
21	  --successful-only      Only clean tasks where result==Success. Failures
22	                         stay around for inspection. Recommended.
23	  --group GROUP          Limit `pueue clean` to one group.
24	  --remove-empty-groups  After cleaning, drop groups with zero tasks.
25	                         Skips `default` (cannot be removed). Skips groups
26	                         currently holding non-Done tasks.
27	  --logs-older-than N    Delete log files older than N days from the
28	                         platform log dir (~/Library/Application Support/
29	                         pueue/logs on macOS, ~/.local/share/pueue/logs on
30	                         Linux). Files for ids still in `pueue status` are
31	                         preserved.
32	  --dry-run              Print what would be done; touch nothing.
33	  --json                 Emit JSON to stdout (default; flag kept for symmetry).
34	  --help, -h             Show this help and exit.
35	
36	Examples:
37	  cleanup.sh --successful-only --remove-empty-groups
38	  cleanup.sh --group dag-abc12345 --logs-older-than 30
39	  cleanup.sh --dry-run --successful-only --logs-older-than 7
40	
41	Exit codes:
42	  0  success (or dry-run)
43	  1  invalid arguments
44	  2  pueue CLI not installed
45	  3  pueued unreachable
46	EOF
47	}
48	
49	log()  { printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2; }
50	warn() { printf 'warn: %s\n' "$*" >&2; }
51	die()  { printf 'error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit "${2:-1}"; }
52	
53	SUCCESS_ONLY=0
54	GROUP=""
55	REMOVE_EMPTY=0
56	LOGS_DAYS=""
57	DRY_RUN=0
58	
59	while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
60	  case "$1" in
61	    --successful-only)     SUCCESS_ONLY=1; shift ;;
62	    --group)               [ $# -ge 2 ] || die "--group requires a value" 1
63	                           GROUP="$2"; shift 2 ;;
64	    --remove-empty-groups) REMOVE_EMPTY=1; shift ;;
65	    --logs-older-than)     [ $# -ge 2 ] || die "--logs-older-than requires N" 1
66	                           LOGS_DAYS="$2"; shift 2 ;;
67	    --dry-run)             DRY_RUN=1; shift ;;
68	    --json)                shift ;;
69	    --help|-h)             usage; exit 0 ;;
70	    *)                     die "unknown flag: $1 (try --help)" 1 ;;
71	  esac
72	done
73	
74	command -v pueue >/dev/null 2>&1 || { log "pueue not installed"; exit 2; }
75	
76	if ! pueue status --json >/dev/null 2>&1; then
77	  log "pueued unreachable. Start with: pueued -d"
78	  exit 3
79	fi
80	
81	# --- Detect platform log dir.
82	PLATFORM=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
83	case "$PLATFORM" in
84	  darwin) LOG_DIR="${HOME}/Library/Application Support/pueue/logs" ;;
85	  linux)  LOG_DIR="${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/pueue/logs" ;;
86	  *)      LOG_DIR="" ;;
87	esac
88	
89	# --- Snapshot pre-cleanup state.
90	PRE_STATUS=$(pueue status --json)
91	
92	# --- 1. Clean tasks (pueue handles its own log files for cleaned tasks).
93	CLEANED_IDS_JSON='[]'
94	if [ "$SUCCESS_ONLY" = "1" ] || [ -n "$GROUP" ] || [ "$DRY_RUN" = "0" ]; then
95	  CLEAN_ARGS=("clean")
96	  [ "$SUCCESS_ONLY" = "1" ] && CLEAN_ARGS+=("--successful-only")
97	  [ -n "$GROUP" ]           && CLEAN_ARGS+=("--group" "$GROUP")
98	
99	  # Compute which ids would be cleaned (pueue clean has no --dry-run).
100	  CLEANED_IDS_JSON=$(printf '%s' "$PRE_STATUS" | \
101	    SUCC="$SUCCESS_ONLY" GRP="$GROUP" python3 -c '
102	import json, os, sys
103	d = json.loads(sys.stdin.read())
104	succ_only = os.environ["SUCC"] == "1"
105	group = os.environ["GRP"]
106	ids = []
107	for tid, t in d.get("tasks", {}).items():
108	    status = t.get("status") or {}
109	    if "Done" not in status: continue
110	    if group and t.get("group") != group: continue
111	    if succ_only and status["Done"].get("result") != "Success": continue
112	    ids.append(int(tid))
113	print(json.dumps(sorted(ids)))
114	')
115	  if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "0" ]; then
116	    pueue "${CLEAN_ARGS[@]}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || warn "pueue clean failed"
117	  fi
118	fi
119	
120	# --- 2. Remove empty non-default groups.
121	REMOVED_GROUPS_JSON='[]'
122	if [ "$REMOVE_EMPTY" = "1" ]; then
123	  POST_STATUS=$(pueue status --json)
124	  REMOVED_GROUPS_JSON=$(printf '%s' "$POST_STATUS" | DRY="$DRY_RUN" python3 -c '
125	import json, os, subprocess, sys
126	d = json.loads(sys.stdin.read())
127	dry = os.environ["DRY"] == "1"
128	removed = []
129	groups = d.get("groups", {})
130	tasks = d.get("tasks", {})
131	# Count tasks per group
132	counts = {}
133	for t in tasks.values():
134	    counts[t.get("group", "default")] = counts.get(t.get("group", "default"), 0) + 1
135	for g in groups:
136	    if g == "default": continue
137	    if counts.get(g, 0) > 0: continue
138	    if not dry:
139	        r = subprocess.run(["pueue", "group", "remove", g],
140	                           capture_output=True, text=True)
141	        if r.returncode == 0:
142	            removed.append(g)
143	    else:
144	        removed.append(g)
145	print(json.dumps(sorted(removed)))
146	')
147	fi
148	
149	# --- 3. Delete old log files (only those whose id is no longer in status).
150	DELETED_LOGS_JSON='[]'
151	if [ -n "$LOGS_DAYS" ] && [ -n "$LOG_DIR" ] && [ -d "$LOG_DIR" ]; then
152	  POST_STATUS=$(pueue status --json)
153	  DELETED_LOGS_JSON=$(LD="$LOG_DIR" DAYS="$LOGS_DAYS" DRY="$DRY_RUN" \
154	    POST="$POST_STATUS" python3 -c '
155	import json, os, sys, time
156	import pathlib
157	log_dir = pathlib.Path(os.environ["LD"])
158	days = int(os.environ["DAYS"])
159	dry = os.environ["DRY"] == "1"
160	status = json.loads(os.environ["POST"])
161	live_ids = set(status.get("tasks", {}).keys())
162	cutoff = time.time() - days * 86400
163	deleted = []
164	for f in log_dir.glob("*.log"):
165	    stem = f.stem
166	    if stem in live_ids:
167	        continue  # log file for a still-tracked task; skip
168	    try:
169	        if f.stat().st_mtime > cutoff:
170	            continue
171	    except OSError:
172	        continue
173	    if not dry:
174	        try: f.unlink()
175	        except OSError: continue
176	    deleted.append(str(f))
177	print(json.dumps(sorted(deleted)))
178	')
179	fi
180	
181	# --- 4. Emit report.
182	PRE_STATUS_FOR_RUNNING="$PRE_STATUS" \
183	CLEANED="$CLEANED_IDS_JSON" \
184	REMOVED="$REMOVED_GROUPS_JSON" \
185	DELETED="$DELETED_LOGS_JSON" \
186	DRY="$DRY_RUN" \
187	LOG_DIR_OUT="$LOG_DIR" \
188	python3 <<'PY'
189	import json, os
190	pre = json.loads(os.environ["PRE_STATUS_FOR_RUNNING"])
191	running = sorted(int(tid) for tid, t in pre.get("tasks", {}).items()
192	                 if isinstance(t.get("status"), dict) and "Done" not in t["status"])
193	print(json.dumps({
194	    "cleaned_tasks": json.loads(os.environ["CLEANED"]),
195	    "removed_groups": json.loads(os.environ["REMOVED"]),
196	    "deleted_logs": json.loads(os.environ["DELETED"]),
197	    "kept_running": running,
198	    "log_dir": os.environ["LOG_DIR_OUT"],
199	    "dry_run": os.environ["DRY"] == "1",
200	}))
201	PY
202

```text
1	# pueue CLI cheatsheet
2	
3	The skill's wrapper scripts cover **submit / DAG / wait**. Everything else is
4	fine to call directly. This page lists the un-wrapped commands the agent
5	should reach for, with one-line "when to use" notes.
6	
7	Always run `pueue <subcmd> --help` first if anything below looks ambiguous —
8	flags occasionally change between releases.
9	
10	## Inspecting state
11	
12	| Command | When to use |
13	|---|---|
14	| `pueue status` | Quick human-readable view. Pretty table with deps, group, label, start/end. |
15	| `pueue status --json` | Machine-readable. The agent's primary status surface. See `references/json-schema.md`. |
16	| `pueue status [QUERY]` | SQL-ish filter: `pueue status 'status=Failed'`, `pueue status 'columns=[id,label,end] order_by end desc'`. Run `pueue status --help` for grammar. Usable with `--json`. |
17	| `pueue group` | List groups with their parallelism settings (table form). |
18	| `pueue group --json` | Same, JSON. Shape: `{"<name>": {"status": "Running", "parallel_tasks": N}}`. |
19	| `pueue log <id>` | Last few lines of stdout/stderr. `--lines N` for more. `--full` for everything. |
20	| `pueue log --json --full <id>` | Full log payload as JSON. The output field is the captured stdout/stderr. |
21	| `pueue follow <id>` | `tail -f` against a running task. Blocks. Ctrl-C to detach. |
22	| `pueue follow --stderr <id>` | Same but stderr only (rarely useful — pueue captures both into one stream by default). |
23	
24	## Lifecycle
25	
26	| Command | When to use |
27	|---|---|
28	| `pueue start [<ids>]` | Resume one or more paused tasks (or `--group G` to resume a whole group). |
29	| `pueue pause [<ids>]` | Pause tasks (or `--group G` for a whole group). The task keeps running its current step until SIGSTOP-able point. |
30	| `pueue kill <ids>` | Send SIGKILL. Status becomes `Done.Killed`. |
31	| `pueue kill --group G` | Kill everything in a group. |
32	| `pueue remove <ids>` | Drop terminated tasks from the visible list. **Each id must be a separate arg** — bash arrays, not space-joined strings. |
33	| `pueue clean` | Remove ALL finished tasks from the visible list. Includes failures. Be deliberate. |
34	| `pueue clean --successful-only` | Keep failures around for inspection; drop successes. |
35	| `pueue reset` | Nuclear option: kill everything, clear the list, reset state. Survives daemon restart. |
36	| `pueue shutdown` | Stop `pueued` cleanly. State is persisted to disk. |
37	
38	## Retrying and editing
39	
40	| Command | When to use |
41	|---|---|
42	| `pueue restart <ids>` | Re-enqueue with a NEW task id. The old id stays in history with its old result. |
43	| `pueue restart --in-place <ids>` | Reuse the same id. Overwrites the old log. Most agents want this for "retry this". |
44	| `pueue restart --all-failed` | Restart every failed task (across all groups). Pair with `--in-place` if you want to reuse ids. |
45	| `pueue restart --failed-in-group G` | Like `--all-failed` but scoped to one group. |
46	| `pueue restart --start-immediately <ids>` (alias `-k`) | Bypass queue + dependencies; start now. |
47	| `pueue restart --stashed <ids>` | Restart but in Stashed state (won't auto-run; you `pueue enqueue` later). |
48	| `pueue edit <id>` | Open `$EDITOR` to modify the command, path, label, etc. of an enqueued task. |
49	| `pueue env <id> <add\|remove\|list>` | Adjust a task's environment variables before it runs. |
50	| `pueue stash <ids>` | Move tasks to Stashed state (won't auto-start). |
51	| `pueue enqueue <ids>` | Move stashed tasks back to Queued. Optional `--delay STR`. |
52	| `pueue switch <id1> <id2>` | Swap queue positions (rarely needed; priority is usually cleaner). |
53	
54	## Groups and parallelism
55	
56	| Command | When to use |
57	|---|---|
58	| `pueue group add <name>` | Create a new group. `default` already exists. |
59	| `pueue group remove <name>` | Delete. **Tasks in the group move to `default`** — they don't disappear. |
60	| `pueue parallel <N>` | Set parallelism for the default group. `0` = unlimited. |
61	| `pueue parallel <N> --group G` | Set parallelism for a specific group. |
62	
63	## Sending input to running tasks
64	
65	| Command | When to use |
66	|---|---|
67	| `pueue send <id> "y\n"` | Pipe a string to the task's stdin. Useful for confirmations on interactive scripts. |
68	
69	## Daemon
70	
71	| Command | When to use |
72	|---|---|
73	| `pueued -d` | Start daemon (forks). |
74	| `pueued -d --config PATH` | Start with a non-default config (e.g. a test fixture). |
75	| `pueued -v -d` | Verbose stderr — debug startup issues. |
76	| `PUEUE_CONFIG_PATH=... pueue ...` | Point the client at a non-default config. Pair with `pueued -d --config PATH` for isolated test daemons. |
77	
78	## Completions
79	
80	`pueue completions <shell> <out-dir>` — generate shell completions. Run
81	once on setup if your shell isn't autocompleting.
82	
83	## What this skill DOES wrap
84	
85	- `pueue add` (`scripts/submit.sh` — JSON-output wrapper, group autocreate, defensive id parse)
86	- `pueue add` for DAGs (`scripts/submit-dag.py` — declarative spec, topo sort, validation)
87	- `pueue status --json` polling for "block until terminal" semantics (`scripts/wait.py`)
88	- Daemon health probe (`scripts/check-daemon.sh`)
89	
90	Everything else, call directly.
91

````text
1	# Driving a remote pueued
2	
3	Pueue can't schedule *across* hosts (that's Slurm / K8s / Ray territory), but a
4	local `pueue` client **can** drive a `pueued` on another machine — and it gets
5	full control, not read-only status: `add`, `kill`, `log`, `follow` all work.
6	
7	Whether you should is a different question. Read "Just SSH over instead" first.
8	
9	> Everything below was verified against a real macOS client (pueue 4.0.4)
10	> driving a Linux `pueued` (4.0.2) over SSH unix-socket forwarding.
11	
12	## Just SSH over instead
13	
14	For most work, this is the correct answer and needs no setup at all:
15	
16	```bash
17	ssh myhost 'pueue add --label train-seed1 -- ./train.sh'
18	ssh myhost 'pueue status --json' | jq .
19	```
20	
21	The remote client runs on the remote box, so paths, environment, and logs are
22	all consistent. Nothing to configure, no secret to copy, no cert to sync.
23	
24	Reach for a real remote connection only when you want **local composition** —
25	a `pueue status --json` you can pipe straight into `jq` without an SSH round
26	trip per call, or a script/agent that shells out to `pueue` many times.
27	
28	Even then, the upstream wiki steers you away from exposing the daemon:
29	
30	> "If that's not safe enough for your use-case, you can always listen on
31	> unix-sockets/localhost and do port/unix-socket forwarding via SSH."
32	
33	So the recommended setup is **SSH forwarding**, below. Direct TCP exposure is
34	the last resort, not the default.
35	
36	## Recommended: SSH unix-socket forwarding
37	
38	The daemon keeps its default unix socket and **needs no reconfiguration** —
39	you change nothing on the server. Only the client gets a config.
40	
41	### 1. Find the daemon's socket
42	
43	```bash
44	ssh myhost 'ls /run/user/$(id -u)/pueue_*.socket'
45	# /run/user/1000/pueue_myuser.socket
46	```
47	
48	`unix_socket_path: null` in the server's config means this default location.
49	
50	### 2. Copy the shared secret
51	
52	The client authenticates with the *same* secret file as the daemon:
53	
54	```bash
55	mkdir -p ~/.config/pueue/remote && chmod 700 ~/.config/pueue/remote
56	ssh myhost 'cat ~/.local/share/pueue/shared_secret' > ~/.config/pueue/remote/shared_secret
57	chmod 600 ~/.config/pueue/remote/shared_secret
58	```
59	
60	### 3. Write a client-only config
61	
62	Keep it separate from your local config and select it with `-c`:
63	
64	```yaml
65	# ~/.config/pueue/remote/client.yml
66	client:
67	  read_local_logs: false          # REQUIRED — see Gotchas
68	shared:
69	  use_unix_socket: true
70	  unix_socket_path: /home/you/.config/pueue/remote/remote.sock
71	  shared_secret_path: /home/you/.config/pueue/remote/shared_secret
72	```
73	
74	### 4. Forward the socket, then talk to it
75	
76	```bash
77	ssh -f -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
78	    -L ~/.config/pueue/remote/remote.sock:/run/user/1000/pueue_myuser.socket \
79	    myhost
80	
81	pueue -c ~/.config/pueue/remote/client.yml status
82	```
83	
84	Add `-o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3` for a long-lived
85	tunnel, or manage it with `autossh` / a systemd user unit. Remove the stale
86	local socket file before re-forwarding.
87	
88	Because the tunnel terminates at the daemon's own unix socket, **no TLS
89	certificate is involved** — the `daemon_cert` / TCP plumbing below only applies
90	if you skip SSH.
91	
92	## Alternative: direct TCP + TLS
93	
94	Only if SSH forwarding genuinely doesn't fit. Requires editing the server's
95	config and **restarting `pueued`**, which interrupts a running queue.
96	
97	On the daemon: `use_unix_socket: false`, plus a reachable `host` and `port`.
98	Pueue self-signs a TLS certificate at startup; the client verifies against a
99	copy of it:
100	
101	| Client key | Points at |
102	|---|---|
103	| `shared_secret_path` | copy of the daemon's `shared_secret` |
104	| `daemon_cert` | copy of the daemon's `daemon.cert` |
105	| `host` / `port` | the daemon's listen address |
106	| `use_unix_socket: false` | required |
107	
108	The client "will only connect to a pueued daemon which serves the known
109	certificate", so the cert must be re-copied whenever the daemon regenerates it.
110	
111	## Gotchas
112	
113	- **`read_local_logs: false` is mandatory on a remote client.** Left at the
114	  default `true`, the client tries to read task logs off its *own* disk, where
115	  the remote daemon's log directory does not exist. Set it false and logs come
116	  back over the connection instead. `log` and `follow` were verified working
117	  this way.
118	
119	- **The working directory is resolved on the CLIENT, and this is the thing
120	  that will bite you.** Pueue records a task's cwd at submit time and
````
